"In the sacred relationship between the dreamer's body and the cathedral, he finds an immediate complement in the profane preoccupations of his waking life. The passage I was listening to now referred to Erasmus - previously sketched in the Enchiridion, later defined in the polemic against Luther in the Hyperaspites, and vulgarized in the Ecclesiastes - and assuredly, we must look to the Ratio for its fundamental exposition. Familiar Colloquies demonstrated the reason for the inclusion of the Greek text when defending his work: 'But one thing the facts cry out, and it can be clear, as they say, even to a blind man, that often through the translator's clumsiness or inattention the Greek has been wrongly rendered; often the translator has not understood the meaning of the Greek, and has thus falsified the text.' The hermeneutical principle of scripture, as Erasmus stated it, was: 'the middle is the medium, the medium is the mediator, the mediator is the reconciler.' In Erasmus' early Enchiridion, he had given this scopus in typical medieval terms of an ascent of being. The Paraphrases of Erasmus (1517-1524), the first tome or volume of the Paraphrase of Erasmus upon the newe testamente (1548), were not translations but something looser, a kind of commentary in which the writer and his author retained separate roles. The Paraphrases allowed Erasmus to amplify the text of the New Testament by integrating philological and theological points from his scholarly annotations. In effect, like sacraments, reading them becomes a form of prayer which is spoiled by taking single sentences in isolation and using them as syllogisms. Instead, learning to understand the genres and literary expression in the New Testament becomes a spiritual exercise. Erasmus' approach has been called rhetorical, but it is also deeply devotional."
